(Surat al-Nazi'at)
(It has forty-six verses and is Meccan)
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
﴿By those who drag forth violently,﴾ ﴿by those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿by those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race forward,﴾ ﴿then those who arrange affairs.﴾
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)
﴿By those who drag forth violently,﴾ ﴿by those who draw out gently,﴾ ﴿by those who glide swiftly,﴾ ﴿then those who race forward,﴾ ﴿then those who arrange affairs.﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first issue: Know that these five words may be attributes of one thing, and may not be so. As for the first possibility, they have mentioned several opinions regarding the verse:

(The first) that they are all attributes of the angels. So His saying ﴿By those who drag forth violently﴾ refers to the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. When they pull out the soul of an unbeliever, they pull it with severity. This is derived from their saying: "nazaʿa fi al-qaws fa-aghraqa" (he drew the bowstring and over-drew it). It is said: "aghraqa al-nazii' fi al-qaws" when the archer reaches the utmost limit of the draw, until it reaches the arrow-head. So the sense of the verse is: "by those who draw with over-drawing (ighraq)." Al-gharq and al-ighraq are, in the language, of one meaning. His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾: al-nashṭ is pulling. It is said: "nashaṭtu al-dalw, unshiṭuhā, wa-anshaṭtuhā nashṭan" — I drew the bucket out gently. The meaning is the angels who draw out the soul of the believer and take it gently. We have specified this for the believer and the first for the unbeliever because of the difference between drawing violently and drawing gently: al-nazʿ is pulling with severity, and al-nashṭ is pulling with gentleness and softness. So the angels draw out the souls of the believers just as the bucket is drawn out of the well. The conclusion is that His saying ﴿By those who drag forth violently, by those who draw out gently﴾ is an oath by the Angel of Death and his assistants, except that the first indicates the manner of taking the souls of the unbelievers, and the second indicates the manner of taking the souls of the believers.

As for His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾, some have restricted it also to the angels who take souls, and some have taken it to refer to the rest of the categories of angels.

As for the first opinion, it is transmitted from ʿAlī (peace be upon him), Ibn ʿAbbās, and Masrūq that the angels draw out the souls of the believers with gentle drawing. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾. Then they leave it to rest for a while, then they extract it afterward with gentleness and delicacy, like one who swims in water, who moves gently and delicately so as not to sink. Likewise here, they are gentle in this extraction

so that pain and severity do not reach it. That is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾. As for those who took it to refer to the rest of the categories of angels, they said: the angels descend from the heaven swiftly, so their descent from the sky is made like swimming, and the Arabs say of a noble horse that it is "al-sābiḥ" (the swimmer).

As for His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾, some have explained it as the angels who take souls, who race forward with the souls of the unbelievers to the Fire, and with the souls of the believers to Paradise. Others have explained it as the rest of the categories of angels. Then they mentioned several opinions regarding this racing:

(The first) Mujahid and Abu Rawq said: the angels precede the son of Adam in faith and obedience, and there is no doubt that racing in good deeds is a great rank. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost, ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 10–11].

(The second) al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: the angels outpace the devils with revelation to the prophets, because the devils used to steal hearing.

(The third) and it is possible that the meaning is that He the Exalted described them, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 27], meaning before permission they do not move or speak, out of glorification of the majesty of Allah the Exalted and fear of His awe. Here He described them with racing, meaning when the command comes to them, they hasten to carry it out and rush to show their obedience. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾.

As for His saying ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, they agreed that they are the angels. Muqatil said: meaning Jibril, Mikail, Israfil and ʿAzrāʾīl, peace be upon them, who arrange the command of Allah the Exalted concerning the people of the earth, and they are "the distributors of affairs." As for Jibril, he is entrusted with the winds and the hosts; as for Mikail, he is entrusted with rain and plants; as for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with taking souls; as for Israfil, he descends with the command to them. Among them are a group entrusted with guarding the children of Adam, another group with recording their deeds, and another group with sinking, transformation, winds, clouds and rains.

Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: Why did He say ﴿those who arrange affairs (amran)﴾ and not "affairs (umūran)," since they arrange many affairs and not one single affair? (The answer): the intended meaning is the genus, and when it is so, it stands in place of the plural.

The second question: He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the command is all for Allah﴾, so how does He here establish for them the arranging of the affair? (The answer): since that bringing [of it] is what they do, the command is as if it were His. This is a summary of what the exegetes have said on this topic. But I have here another opinion, which is that the angels have negative attributes and relational attributes. As for the negative attributes, they are free from desire, anger, blameworthy traits, death, old age, sickness, composition of organs, humors and elements. Rather, they are spiritual substances free from these states. So His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates that they are wholly stripped of these states in every respect. On this interpretation, "al-nāziʿāt" are the ones possessing extraction, like "al-Labin" and "al-Tamir." As for His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾, it indicates that their departure from these states is not by way of obligation and hardship as with humans, but rather by the requirement of their quiddities they have departed from these states and are exalted above these attributes. These two words are thus indications describing their negative states. As for their relational attributes, they are of two kinds: (one of them) is an explanation of their intellectual faculty, that is, how their state is in knowing the kingdom and dominion of Allah and in being informed of the light of His majesty. So He described them in this station with two descriptions: (one of them) is His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾, for they glide from the beginning of their nature in the seas of Allah's majesty, and then there is no end to their gliding, because there is no end to Allah's greatness, the loftiness of His self-sufficiency, the light of His majesty and His magnificence. So they are forever in that gliding. (The second) is His saying

﴿then those who race forward﴾, which is an indication of the ranks of the angels in that gliding. For just as the ranks of the knowledge of animals compared to the ranks of the knowledge of humans are deficient, and the ranks of the knowledge of humans compared to the ranks of the knowledge of angels are deficient, so too the knowledge of some of those angels compared to the ranks of knowledge of the others varies. And just as the difference between the species of the horse and the species of the human is in quiddity and not in accidents, so too the difference between the individual of each angel and the individual of another is in quiddity. So when their individuals vary in quiddity and not in accidents, they will necessarily vary in degrees of knowledge and in levels of manifestation. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾. These two words are intended to explain the state of their intellectual faculty.
* * *
As for His saying ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, it is an indication of explaining the state of their active faculty, because every state of the lower world is entrusted to the management of one of the angels who are the inhabitants of the upper world and the dwellers of the regions of the heavens. And since management is not completed except after knowledge, they necessarily put the explanation of the intellectual faculty they have before the explanation of the active faculty they have. This which I have mentioned is an apparent possibility, and Allah knows best His intended meaning in His words.

Know that Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani objected to interpreting these words as referring to the angels, and said: the singular of "al-nāziʿāt" is "nāziʿa," which is of feminine form, and Allah the Exalted has declared the angels free from femininity, and He censured the saying of the unbelievers when He said: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Gracious, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19].

Know that this objection does not apply to our interpretation, because the intended meaning is things possessing extraction, and this measure does not require the feminine as mentioned.

The second opinion regarding the interpretation of these words: that they are the stars. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. Describing the stars as "al-nāziʿāt" admits of several possibilities:

(The first) as if they are drawn from beneath the earth and are attracted to what is above the earth. When they are drawn, they become possessors of extraction, so it is correct to say they are "nāziʿa," on the analogy of "al-Labin" and "al-Tamir."

(The second) that "al-nāziʿāt" derives from their saying "nazaʿa ilayhi," meaning he went with a going-out. Thus al-Wahidi said. So it is as if they rise and set by drawing and driving.

(The third) that it is from their saying: "nazaʿat al-khayl" when horses ran, so the meaning of "wa-al-nāziʿāt" is "and those running at the appointed pace and the fixed limit." As for His saying "gharqan," it admits of two aspects:

(One of them) that it be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of "al-nāziʿāt," meaning these stars are like those drowned in that drawing and intent. This is an indication of the perfection of their state in that intent. If it is said: if the spheres and stars are not living rational beings, what is the meaning of describing them thus? We say: this is by way of comparison, like His saying: ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Yasin: 40], for the plural with waw and nun is for rational beings, and then it was mentioned of the stars by way of comparison.

(The second) that the meaning of their "drowning" is their disappearance in the horizon of the west. So "al-nāziʿāt" is an indication of their rising, and "gharqan" is an indication of their setting, that is, they draw and then are drowned with drowning. This aspect has been mentioned by a group of exegetes.

As for His saying ﴿and those who glide swiftly, gliding (nashṭan)﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: its meaning is that they go out from one mansion to another, from your saying: "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. I say: the upshot of this statement returns to: His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates their daily motion, and ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾ indicates their movement from one mansion to another, which is their particular motion in their own spheres. And it is remarkable that their daily motions are compulsory, while their motion from mansion to mansion is not compulsory, but

agreeable to their essences. Therefore He called the former "nazʿ" and the latter "nashṭ." So reflect, O poor one, upon these secrets.
* * *
As for His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly, gliding﴾, al-Hasan and Abu ʿUbayda, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: they are the stars swimming in the sphere, because their passage through the air is like swimming. For this reason He said: ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Yasin: 40].
* * *
As for His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾, al-Hasan and Abu ʿUbayda said: they are the stars, some of which outpace others in motion, because some of them have a faster movement than others, or because of their retrogression or their direct motion.

As for the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, there are two aspects:

(One of them) that by means of their course and movement, some times are distinguished from others, so the times of worship appear, as He the Exalted said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him is praise﴾ [al-Rum: 17–18], and He said: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: they are times for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], and He said: ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5]. And because by the motion of the sun the four seasons differ, and by their variation the conditions of people's livelihood differ, therefore these managements are rightly attributed to them.

(Second) Once it has been established by proof that every body is originated (ḥādith), it follows that the stars are originated and in need of one who brings them into existence and of a Maker who creates them. Then, even if we suppose that their Maker deposited in them powers that affect the conditions of this world, this would not undermine religion at all, even if we do not affirm that these powers exist. We say instead that God, glorified and exalted, has made His custom to be that each of their particular states becomes a cause for a particular event in this world, just as He made eating a cause of satiety, drinking a cause of quenching thirst, and contact with fire a cause of burning. Holding this view does not harm Islam in any way whatsoever. God knows best the reality of the matter.

The third aspect in interpreting these five words is that they refer to souls (arwāḥ). This is because the soul of the dead person is pulled out (tanzi'u). One says: "So-and-so is in the throes of death (al-nazʿ)," and "So-and-so is being pulled out (yanzi'u)" when he is in the death agony (siyāq al-mawt). "The souls are pulling out (nāzi'āt) at the time of the death agony." The meaning of "gharqan" is a forceful pulling, the most intense and extreme, like the archer's drawing of the bow to its full extent (ighrāq al-nāzi' fī al-qaws). Likewise "tanshiṭu," because nashṭ means departure (al-khurūj). Then, the human souls, free of bodily attachments and longing for union with the higher realm, once they have departed from the darkness of bodies, go to the world of the angels and the abodes of holiness (qudus) in the swiftest manner, in repose and fragrance. So their departure in this state is expressed by the word "swimming" (sibāḥa). Moreover, there is no doubt that the ranks of souls differ in their aversion to this world and their love of union with the higher world. The more perfect they are in these states, the earlier their journey there; the weaker they are, the heavier their journey there. There is no doubt that the souls that are first to attain these states are the most noble. Therefore, the oath is sworn by them. Furthermore, it is not unlikely that among these noble, exalted souls there are some which, because of their strength and nobility, leave visible effects on the conditions of this world. Thus they are "those who arrange affairs" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾, "those who arrange the matter"). Does not a person see his teacher in a dream, ask him about a problem, and be guided to its solution? Does not a son see his father in a dream, and be guided to a buried treasure? Did not Galen (Jālīnūs) say: "I was sick and could not treat myself, so I saw someone in a dream who guided me to the method of treatment"? Did not al-Ghazali say: "When noble souls separate from their bodies, and then a person who resembles the first person in soul and body appears, it is not unlikely that the separated soul acquires an attachment to this body, until it becomes like a helper to the soul attached to that body in acts of goodness; and that assistance is called inspiration (ilhām)." The counterpart of this among wicked souls is whispering (waswasa). Although these meanings are not transmitted from the exegetes, the word is highly capable of bearing them.

The fourth aspect in interpreting these five words: they are attributes of the horses of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) refers to them because they pull at their reins with such force that the reins are drawn out, owing to the length of their necks, because they are purebred (ʿirāb). "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) refers to them because they leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war. It is from the expression "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) refers to them because they swim (sabaḥa) in their running. "Those who race" (sābiqāt) refers to them because they outrun to the finish. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) refers to them as arranging the matter of victory and triumph. Ascribing the arranging to them is metaphorical, because they are among its causes.

* * *

The fifth aspect, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him: these are attributes of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) are the hands of the raiders. One says of the archer "nazaʿa fī qawsihi" (he drew his bow). One says "aghraqa fi al-nazʿ" when he draws the bowstring to its full extent. "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) are the arrows, and their movement is their leaving the hands of the archers and their penetrating. Everything you loosen (ḥalaltahu) you have made active (naššaṭtahu). From this comes nashāṭ al-rajul, which is his expansion and lightness. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) in this context are the horses, and their swimming is their running. It is also permissible to mean camels by it. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) are like "those who follow" (muʿaqqibāt). The meaning is that, after this action, which is the pulling of arrows and the swimming and racing of horses, comes the matter which is victory. The feminine form of the word is because these are groups, as it is said "al-mudabbirāt." It is possible that what is meant is the instrument, namely the bow and the nooses, in the sense of that from which the arrow is drawn and by which the rope is loosed.

The sixth aspect: it is possible to interpret these words by the stations involved in the heart's return from other than God, exalted is He, to God. "By those who pull out forcefully" (﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾) refers to the souls that strive to grasp the firmest handhold (al-ʿurwa al-wuthqā), or those that are drawn away from love of other than God, exalted is He. "And those who move swiftly, with swiftness" (﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾) refers to the fact that, after their return from corporeal things, they begin striving and adorning themselves with the character of God, glorified and exalted, with complete energy and strong power. "And those who swim, with swimming" (﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾): then, after striving, they roam in the matter of the dominion (malakūt), and they traverse those seas and swim in them. "Then those who race, racing" (﴿فالسّابِقاتِ سَبْقًا﴾) is an indication of the differences among souls in their degrees of journeying to God, exalted is He. "Then those who arrange the matter" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾) is an indication that the last stage of humanity is connected to the first degree of angelhood. When human souls reach the furthest of their goals, which is the rank of racing, they are joined to the world of the angels. This is what is meant by His words: "then those who arrange the matter." So the first four are what is meant by His words: "its oil would almost give light" (﴿يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ﴾, Q. 24:35). The fifth is the fire in His words: "even if no fire had touched it" (﴿ولَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ﴾, Q. 24:35).

Know that the aspects transmitted from the exegetes are not transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explicitly, such that no addition to them is possible. Rather, they mentioned them only because the word is capable of bearing them. If the word's capacity for what we have mentioned is not less than its capacity for the aspects they mentioned, then what they mentioned is not preferable to what we mentioned. However, there is a subtle point here: the word is capable of all of them. If we find among these meanings one common concept, we interpret the word according to that common concept, and then all these aspects fall under it. But if there is no common measure among these concepts, it is impossible to interpret the word as covering all of them, because a homonymous word may not be used to convey both of its meanings at once. In that case we do not say: "This is the meaning intended by God, exalted is He." Rather we say: "It is possible that this is what is intended." As for certainty, there is no way to it here.

The second possibility: these five words are not attributes of one single thing, but of different things. In this case too there are aspects:

(First) "Those who pull out forcefully" are the bows; "those who move swiftly" are the nooses; "those who swim" are the ships; "those who race" are the horses; and "those who arrange" are the angels. This was narrated by Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib from ʿAṭāʾ.

(Second) It is reported from Mujahid that "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" are death, and that "those who race" and "those who arrange" are the angels. Ascribing the pulling, the moving, and the swimming to death is metaphorical, in the sense that they occur at its occurrence.

* * *

(Third) Qatada said: all of them are the stars, except "those who arrange," which are the angels.

The second issue: He mentioned "fa-al-sābiqāt" with the fā' (then), while the one before it has the wāw (and). There are two explanations for this:

(First) The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: this clause is a consequence of the one before it, as if it were said: "and those that swam and then raced." The fā' makes swimming the cause of racing, just as you say: "He stood up, then he left," where the fā' establishes that standing was the cause of leaving. If you said "He stood and left," you would not be making standing a cause of leaving. Al-Wahidi said: the view of the author of al-Nazm is not consistent regarding His words "fa-al-mudabbirāt amran," because it is unlikely that racing should be the cause of arranging. I say: the objection of al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, can be answered in two ways:

(First) It is not unlikely to say: when they were commanded, they swam, then raced, then arranged what they were commanded to arrange and set right. These are actions connected one to another, like your saying: "Zayd stood up, then left, then struck ʿAmr."

(Second) It is not unlikely to say: when they were foremost in performing acts of obedience and hastened to them, their trustworthiness became evident. For this reason God entrusted to them the management of part of the world.

(Second explanation) The angels are of two kinds: the chiefs and the disciples. The evidence for this is that God, glorified and exalted, said: "Say: The angel of death will take you back" (﴿قُلْ يَتَوَفّاكم مَلَكُ المَوْتِ﴾, Q. 32:11), and then said: "Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him" (﴿حَتّى إذا جاءَ أحَدَكُمُ المَوْتُ تَوَفَّتْهُ رُسُلُنا﴾, Q. 6:61). We said, in reconciling the two verses, that the angel of death is the head, and the chief and the rest of the angels are his disciples. Having understood this, we say: "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" refer to the disciples who themselves carry out the work. Then His words, exalted is He, "fa-al-sābiqāt... fa-al-mudabbirāt" are an indication of the chiefs, who are foremost in rank and nobility, and who are the arrangers of those states and works.

Muqatil said: meaning Jibril, Mikail, Israfil and ʿAzrāʾīl, peace be upon them, who arrange the command of Allah the Exalted concerning the people of the earth, and they are "the distributors of affairs." As for Jibril, he is entrusted with the winds and the hosts; as for Mikail, he is entrusted with rain and plants; as for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with taking souls; as for Israfil, he descends with the command to them. Among them are a group entrusted with guarding the children of Adam, another group with recording their deeds, and another group with sinking, transformation, winds, clouds and rains.

Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: Why did He say ﴿those who arrange affairs (amran)﴾ and not "affairs (umūran)," since they arrange many affairs and not one single affair? (The answer): the intended meaning is the genus, and when it is so, it stands in place of the plural.

The second question: He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the command is all for Allah﴾, so how does He here establish for them the arranging of the affair? (The answer): since that bringing [of it] is what they do, the command is as if it were His. This is a summary of what the exegetes have said on this topic. But I have here another opinion, which is that the angels have negative attributes and relational attributes. As for the negative attributes, they are free from desire, anger, blameworthy traits, death, old age, sickness, composition of organs, humors and elements. Rather, they are spiritual substances free from these states. So His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates that they are wholly stripped of these states in every respect. On this interpretation, "al-nāziʿāt" are the ones possessing extraction, like "al-Labin" and "al-Tamir." As for His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾, it indicates that their departure from these states is not by way of obligation and hardship as with humans, but rather by the requirement of their quiddities they have departed from these states and are exalted above these attributes. These two words are thus indications describing their negative states. As for their relational attributes, they are of two kinds: (one of them) is an explanation of their intellectual faculty, that is, how their state is in knowing the kingdom and dominion of Allah and in being informed of the light of His majesty. So He described them in this station with two descriptions: (one of them) is His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾, for they glide from the beginning of their nature in the seas of Allah's majesty, and then there is no end to their gliding, because there is no end to Allah's greatness, the loftiness of His self-sufficiency, the light of His majesty and His magnificence. So they are forever in that gliding. (The second) is His saying

﴿then those who race forward﴾, which is an indication of the ranks of the angels in that gliding. For just as the ranks of the knowledge of animals compared to the ranks of the knowledge of humans are deficient, and the ranks of the knowledge of humans compared to the ranks of the knowledge of angels are deficient, so too the knowledge of some of those angels compared to the ranks of knowledge of the others varies. And just as the difference between the species of the horse and the species of the human is in quiddity and not in accidents, so too the difference between the individual of each angel and the individual of another is in quiddity. So when their individuals vary in quiddity and not in accidents, they will necessarily vary in degrees of knowledge and in levels of manifestation. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾. These two words are intended to explain the state of their intellectual faculty.
* * *
As for His saying ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, it is an indication of explaining the state of their active faculty, because every state of the lower world is entrusted to the management of one of the angels who are the inhabitants of the upper world and the dwellers of the regions of the heavens. And since management is not completed except after knowledge, they necessarily put the explanation of the intellectual faculty they have before the explanation of the active faculty they have. This which I have mentioned is an apparent possibility, and Allah knows best His intended meaning in His words.

Know that Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani objected to interpreting these words as referring to the angels, and said: the singular of "al-nāziʿāt" is "nāziʿa," which is of feminine form, and Allah the Exalted has declared the angels free from femininity, and He censured the saying of the unbelievers when He said: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Gracious, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19].

Know that this objection does not apply to our interpretation, because the intended meaning is things possessing extraction, and this measure does not require the feminine as mentioned.

The second opinion regarding the interpretation of these words: that they are the stars. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. Describing the stars as "al-nāziʿāt" admits of several possibilities:

(The first) as if they are drawn from beneath the earth and are attracted to what is above the earth. When they are drawn, they become possessors of extraction, so it is correct to say they are "nāziʿa," on the analogy of "al-Labin" and "al-Tamir."

(The second) that "al-nāziʿāt" derives from their saying "nazaʿa ilayhi," meaning he went with a going-out. Thus al-Wahidi said. So it is as if they rise and set by drawing and driving.

(The third) that it is from their saying: "nazaʿat al-khayl" when horses ran, so the meaning of "wa-al-nāziʿāt" is "and those running at the appointed pace and the fixed limit." As for His saying "gharqan," it admits of two aspects:

(One of them) that it be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of "al-nāziʿāt," meaning these stars are like those drowned in that drawing and intent. This is an indication of the perfection of their state in that intent. If it is said: if the spheres and stars are not living rational beings, what is the meaning of describing them thus? We say: this is by way of comparison, like His saying: ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Yasin: 40], for the plural with waw and nun is for rational beings, and then it was mentioned of the stars by way of comparison.

(The second) that the meaning of their "drowning" is their disappearance in the horizon of the west. So "al-nāziʿāt" is an indication of their rising, and "gharqan" is an indication of their setting, that is, they draw and then are drowned with drowning. This aspect has been mentioned by a group of exegetes.

As for His saying ﴿and those who glide swiftly, gliding (nashṭan)﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: its meaning is that they go out from one mansion to another, from your saying: "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. I say: the upshot of this statement returns to: His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates their daily motion, and ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾ indicates their movement from one mansion to another, which is their particular motion in their own spheres. And it is remarkable that their daily motions are compulsory, while their motion from mansion to mansion is not compulsory, but

agreeable to their essences. Therefore He called the former "nazʿ" and the latter "nashṭ." So reflect, O poor one, upon these secrets.

As for His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly, gliding﴾, al-Hasan and Abu ʿUbayda, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: they are the stars swimming in the sphere, because their passage through the air is like swimming. For this reason He said: ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Yasin: 40].

As for His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾, al-Hasan and Abu ʿUbayda said: they are the stars, some of which outpace others in motion, because some of them have a faster movement than others, or because of their retrogression or their direct motion.

As for the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, there are two aspects:

(One of them) that by means of their course and movement, some times are distinguished from others, so the times of worship appear, as He the Exalted said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him is praise﴾ [al-Rum: 17–18], and He said: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: they are times for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], and He said: ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5]. And because by the motion of the sun the four seasons differ, and by their variation the conditions of people's livelihood differ, therefore these managements are rightly attributed to them.

(Second) Once it has been established by proof that every body is originated (ḥādith), it follows that the stars are originated and in need of one who brings them into existence and of a Maker who creates them. Then, even if we suppose that their Maker deposited in them powers that affect the conditions of this world, this would not undermine religion at all, even if we do not affirm that these powers exist. We say instead that God, glorified and exalted, has made His custom to be that each of their particular states becomes a cause for a particular event in this world, just as He made eating a cause of satiety, drinking a cause of quenching thirst, and contact with fire a cause of burning. Holding this view does not harm Islam in any way whatsoever. God knows best the reality of the matter.

The third aspect in interpreting these five words is that they refer to souls (arwāḥ). This is because the soul of the dead person is pulled out (tanzi'u). One says: "So-and-so is in the throes of death (al-nazʿ)," and "So-and-so is being pulled out (yanzi'u)" when he is in the death agony (siyāq al-mawt). "The souls are pulling out (nāzi'āt) at the time of the death agony." The meaning of "gharqan" is a forceful pulling, the most intense and extreme, like the archer's drawing of the bow to its full extent (ighrāq al-nāzi' fī al-qaws). Likewise "tanshiṭu," because nashṭ means departure (al-khurūj). Then, the human souls, free of bodily attachments and longing for union with the higher realm, once they have departed from the darkness of bodies, go to the world of the angels and the abodes of holiness (qudus) in the swiftest manner, in repose and fragrance. So their departure in this state is expressed by the word "swimming" (sibāḥa). Moreover, there is no doubt that the ranks of souls differ in their aversion to this world and their love of union with the higher world. The more perfect they are in these states, the earlier their journey there; the weaker they are, the heavier their journey there. There is no doubt that the souls that are first to attain these states are the most noble. Therefore, the oath is sworn by them. Furthermore, it is not unlikely that among these noble, exalted souls there are some which, because of their strength and nobility, leave visible effects on the conditions of this world. Thus they are "those who arrange affairs" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾, "those who arrange the matter"). Does not a person see his teacher in a dream, ask him about a problem, and be guided to its solution? Does not a son see his father in a dream, and be guided to a buried treasure? Did not Galen (Jālīnūs) say: "I was sick and could not treat myself, so I saw someone in a dream who guided me to the method of treatment"? Did not al-Ghazali say: "When noble souls separate from their bodies, and then a person who resembles the first person in soul and body appears, it is not unlikely that the separated soul acquires an attachment to this body, until it becomes like a helper to the soul attached to that body in acts of goodness; and that assistance is called inspiration (ilhām)." The counterpart of this among wicked souls is whispering (waswasa). Although these meanings are not transmitted from the exegetes, the word is highly capable of bearing them.

The fourth aspect in interpreting these five words: they are attributes of the horses of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) refers to them because they pull at their reins with such force that the reins are drawn out, owing to the length of their necks, because they are purebred (ʿirāb). "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) refers to them because they leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war. It is from the expression "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) refers to them because they swim (sabaḥa) in their running. "Those who race" (sābiqāt) refers to them because they outrun to the finish. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) refers to them as arranging the matter of victory and triumph. Ascribing the arranging to them is metaphorical, because they are among its causes.

The fifth aspect, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him: these are attributes of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) are the hands of the raiders. One says of the archer "nazaʿa fī qawsihi" (he drew his bow). One says "aghraqa fi al-nazʿ" when he draws the bowstring to its full extent. "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) are the arrows, and their movement is their leaving the hands of the archers and their penetrating. Everything you loosen (ḥalaltahu) you have made active (naššaṭtahu). From this comes nashāṭ al-rajul, which is his expansion and lightness. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) in this context are the horses, and their swimming is their running. It is also permissible to mean camels by it. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) are like "those who follow" (muʿaqqibāt). The meaning is that, after this action, which is the pulling of arrows and the swimming and racing of horses, comes the matter which is victory. The feminine form of the word is because these are groups, as it is said "al-mudabbirāt." It is possible that what is meant is the instrument, namely the bow and the nooses, in the sense of that from which the arrow is drawn and by which the rope is loosed.

The sixth aspect: it is possible to interpret these words by the stations involved in the heart's return from other than God, exalted is He, to God. "By those who pull out forcefully" (﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾) refers to the souls that strive to grasp the firmest handhold (al-ʿurwa al-wuthqā), or those that are drawn away from love of other than God, exalted is He. "And those who move swiftly, with swiftness" (﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾) refers to the fact that, after their return from corporeal things, they begin striving and adorning themselves with the character of God, glorified and exalted, with complete energy and strong power. "And those who swim, with swimming" (﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾): then, after striving, they roam in the matter of the dominion (malakūt), and they traverse those seas and swim in them. "Then those who race, racing" (﴿فالسّابِقاتِ سَبْقًا﴾) is an indication of the differences among souls in their degrees of journeying to God, exalted is He. "Then those who arrange the matter" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾) is an indication that the last stage of humanity is connected to the first degree of angelhood. When human souls reach the furthest of their goals, which is the rank of racing, they are joined to the world of the angels. This is what is meant by His words: "then those who arrange the matter." So the first four are what is meant by His words: "its oil would almost give light" (﴿يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ﴾, Q. 24:35). The fifth is the fire in His words: "even if no fire had touched it" (﴿ولَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ﴾, Q. 24:35).

Know that the aspects transmitted from the exegetes are not transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explicitly, such that no addition to them is possible. Rather, they mentioned them only because the word is capable of bearing them. If the word's capacity for what we have mentioned is not less than its capacity for the aspects they mentioned, then what they mentioned is not preferable to what we mentioned. However, there is a subtle point here: the word is capable of all of them. If we find among these meanings one common concept, we interpret the word according to that common concept, and then all these aspects fall under it. But if there is no common measure among these concepts, it is impossible to interpret the word as covering all of them, because a homonymous word may not be used to convey both of its meanings at once. In that case we do not say: "This is the meaning intended by God, exalted is He." Rather we say: "It is possible that this is what is intended." As for certainty, there is no way to it here.

The second possibility: these five words are not attributes of one single thing, but of different things. In this case too there are aspects:

(First) "Those who pull out forcefully" are the bows; "those who move swiftly" are the nooses; "those who swim" are the ships; "those who race" are the horses; and "those who arrange" are the angels. This was narrated by Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib from ʿAṭāʾ.

(Second) It is reported from Mujahid that "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" are death, and that "those who race" and "those who arrange" are the angels. Ascribing the pulling, the moving, and the swimming to death is metaphorical, in the sense that they occur at its occurrence.

(Third) Qatada said: all of them are the stars, except "those who arrange," which are the angels.

The second issue: He mentioned "fa-al-sābiqāt" with the fā' (then), while the one before it has the wāw (and). There are two explanations for this:

(First) The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: this clause is a consequence of the one before it, as if it were said: "and those that swam and then raced." The fā' makes swimming the cause of racing, just as you say: "He stood up, then he left," where the fā' establishes that standing was the cause of leaving. If you said "He stood and left," you would not be making standing a cause of leaving. Al-Wahidi said: the view of the author of al-Nazm is not consistent regarding His words "fa-al-mudabbirāt amran," because it is unlikely that racing should be the cause of arranging. I say: the objection of al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, can be answered in two ways:

(First) It is not unlikely to say: when they were commanded, they swam, then raced, then arranged what they were commanded to arrange and set right. These are actions connected one to another, like your saying: "Zayd stood up, then left, then struck ʿAmr."

(Second) It is not unlikely to say: when they were foremost in performing acts of obedience and hastened to them, their trustworthiness became evident. For this reason God entrusted to them the management of part of the world.

(Second explanation) The angels are of two kinds: the chiefs and the disciples. The evidence for this is that God, glorified and exalted, said: "Say: The angel of death will take you back" (﴿قُلْ يَتَوَفّاكم مَلَكُ المَوْتِ﴾, Q. 32:11), and then said: "Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him" (﴿حَتّى إذا جاءَ أحَدَكُمُ المَوْتُ تَوَفَّتْهُ رُسُلُنا﴾, Q. 6:61). We said, in reconciling the two verses, that the angel of death is the head, and the chief and the rest of the angels are his disciples. Having understood this, we say: "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" refer to the disciples who themselves carry out the work. Then His words, exalted is He, "fa-al-sābiqāt... fa-al-mudabbirāt" are an indication of the chiefs, who are foremost in rank and nobility, and who are the arrangers of those states and works.

(The first) as if they are drawn from beneath the earth and are attracted to what is above the earth. When they are drawn, they become possessors of extraction, so it is correct to say they are "nāziʿa," on the analogy of "al-Labin" and "al-Tamir."

(The second) that "al-nāziʿāt" derives from their saying "nazaʿa ilayhi," meaning he went with a going-out. Thus al-Wahidi said. So it is as if they rise and set by drawing and driving.

(The third) that it is from their saying: "nazaʿat al-khayl" when horses ran, so the meaning of "wa-al-nāziʿāt" is "and those running at the appointed pace and the fixed limit." As for His saying "gharqan," it admits of two aspects:

(One of them) that it be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of "al-nāziʿāt," meaning these stars are like those drowned in that drawing and intent. This is an indication of the perfection of their state in that intent. If it is said: if the spheres and stars are not living rational beings, what is the meaning of describing them thus? We say: this is by way of comparison, like His saying: ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Yasin: 40], for the plural with waw and nun is for rational beings, and then it was mentioned of the stars by way of comparison.

(The second) that the meaning of their "drowning" is their disappearance in the horizon of the west. So "al-nāziʿāt" is an indication of their rising, and "gharqan" is an indication of their setting, that is, they draw and then are drowned with drowning. This aspect has been mentioned by a group of exegetes.

As for His saying ﴿and those who glide swiftly, gliding (nashṭan)﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: its meaning is that they go out from one mansion to another, from your saying: "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. I say: the upshot of this statement returns to: His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates their daily motion, and ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾ indicates their movement from one mansion to another, which is their particular motion in their own spheres. And it is remarkable that their daily motions are compulsory, while their motion from mansion to mansion is not compulsory, but

agreeable to their essences. Therefore He called the former "nazʿ" and the latter "nashṭ." So reflect, O poor one, upon these secrets.
* * *
As for His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly, gliding﴾, al-Hasan and Abu ʿUbayda, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: they are the stars swimming in the sphere, because their passage through the air is like swimming. For this reason He said: ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Yasin: 40].
* * *
As for His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾, al-Hasan and Abu ʿUbayda said: they are the stars, some of which outpace others in motion, because some of them have a faster movement than others, or because of their retrogression or their direct motion.
* * *
As for the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, there are two aspects:

(One of them) that by means of their course and movement, some times are distinguished from others, so the times of worship appear, as He the Exalted said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him is praise﴾ [al-Rum: 17–18], and He said: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: they are times for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189], and He said: ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5]. And because by the motion of the sun the four seasons differ, and by their variation the conditions of people's livelihood differ, therefore these managements are rightly attributed to them.

(Second) Once it has been established by proof that every body is originated (ḥādith), it follows that the stars are originated and in need of one who brings them into existence and of a Maker who creates them. Then, even if we suppose that their Maker deposited in them powers that affect the conditions of this world, this would not undermine religion at all, even if we do not affirm that these powers exist. We say instead that God, glorified and exalted, has made His custom to be that each of their particular states becomes a cause for a particular event in this world, just as He made eating a cause of satiety, drinking a cause of quenching thirst, and contact with fire a cause of burning. Holding this view does not harm Islam in any way whatsoever. God knows best the reality of the matter.

The third aspect in interpreting these five words is that they refer to souls (arwāḥ). This is because the soul of the dead person is pulled out (tanzi'u). One says: "So-and-so is in the throes of death (al-nazʿ)," and "So-and-so is being pulled out (yanzi'u)" when he is in the death agony (siyāq al-mawt). "The souls are pulling out (nāzi'āt) at the time of the death agony." The meaning of "gharqan" is a forceful pulling, the most intense and extreme, like the archer's drawing of the bow to its full extent (ighrāq al-nāzi' fī al-qaws). Likewise "tanshiṭu," because nashṭ means departure (al-khurūj). Then, the human souls, free of bodily attachments and longing for union with the higher realm, once they have departed from the darkness of bodies, go to the world of the angels and the abodes of holiness (qudus) in the swiftest manner, in repose and fragrance. So their departure in this state is expressed by the word "swimming" (sibāḥa). Moreover, there is no doubt that the ranks of souls differ in their aversion to this world and their love of union with the higher world. The more perfect they are in these states, the earlier their journey there; the weaker they are, the heavier their journey there. There is no doubt that the souls that are first to attain these states are the most noble. Therefore, the oath is sworn by them. Furthermore, it is not unlikely that among these noble, exalted souls there are some which, because of their strength and nobility, leave visible effects on the conditions of this world. Thus they are "those who arrange affairs" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾, "those who arrange the matter"). Does not a person see his teacher in a dream, ask him about a problem, and be guided to its solution? Does not a son see his father in a dream, and be guided to a buried treasure? Did not Galen (Jālīnūs) say: "I was sick and could not treat myself, so I saw someone in a dream who guided me to the method of treatment"? Did not al-Ghazali say: "When noble souls separate from their bodies, and then a person who resembles the first person in soul and body appears, it is not unlikely that the separated soul acquires an attachment to this body, until it becomes like a helper to the soul attached to that body in acts of goodness; and that assistance is called inspiration (ilhām)." The counterpart of this among wicked souls is whispering (waswasa). Although these meanings are not transmitted from the exegetes, the word is highly capable of bearing them.

The fourth aspect in interpreting these five words: they are attributes of the horses of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) refers to them because they pull at their reins with such force that the reins are drawn out, owing to the length of their necks, because they are purebred (ʿirāb). "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) refers to them because they leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war. It is from the expression "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) refers to them because they swim (sabaḥa) in their running. "Those who race" (sābiqāt) refers to them because they outrun to the finish. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) refers to them as arranging the matter of victory and triumph. Ascribing the arranging to them is metaphorical, because they are among its causes.

* * *

The fifth aspect, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him: these are attributes of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) are the hands of the raiders. One says of the archer "nazaʿa fī qawsihi" (he drew his bow). One says "aghraqa fi al-nazʿ" when he draws the bowstring to its full extent. "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) are the arrows, and their movement is their leaving the hands of the archers and their penetrating. Everything you loosen (ḥalaltahu) you have made active (naššaṭtahu). From this comes nashāṭ al-rajul, which is his expansion and lightness. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) in this context are the horses, and their swimming is their running. It is also permissible to mean camels by it. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) are like "those who follow" (muʿaqqibāt). The meaning is that, after this action, which is the pulling of arrows and the swimming and racing of horses, comes the matter which is victory. The feminine form of the word is because these are groups, as it is said "al-mudabbirāt." It is possible that what is meant is the instrument, namely the bow and the nooses, in the sense of that from which the arrow is drawn and by which the rope is loosed.

The sixth aspect: it is possible to interpret these words by the stations involved in the heart's return from other than God, exalted is He, to God. "By those who pull out forcefully" (﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾) refers to the souls that strive to grasp the firmest handhold (al-ʿurwa al-wuthqā), or those that are drawn away from love of other than God, exalted is He. "And those who move swiftly, with swiftness" (﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾) refers to the fact that, after their return from corporeal things, they begin striving and adorning themselves with the character of God, glorified and exalted, with complete energy and strong power. "And those who swim, with swimming" (﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾): then, after striving, they roam in the matter of the dominion (malakūt), and they traverse those seas and swim in them. "Then those who race, racing" (﴿فالسّابِقاتِ سَبْقًا﴾) is an indication of the differences among souls in their degrees of journeying to God, exalted is He. "Then those who arrange the matter" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾) is an indication that the last stage of humanity is connected to the first degree of angelhood. When human souls reach the furthest of their goals, which is the rank of racing, they are joined to the world of the angels. This is what is meant by His words: "then those who arrange the matter." So the first four are what is meant by His words: "its oil would almost give light" (﴿يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ﴾, Q. 24:35). The fifth is the fire in His words: "even if no fire had touched it" (﴿ولَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ﴾, Q. 24:35).

Know that the aspects transmitted from the exegetes are not transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explicitly, such that no addition to them is possible. Rather, they mentioned them only because the word is capable of bearing them. If the word's capacity for what we have mentioned is not less than its capacity for the aspects they mentioned, then what they mentioned is not preferable to what we mentioned. However, there is a subtle point here: the word is capable of all of them. If we find among these meanings one common concept, we interpret the word according to that common concept, and then all these aspects fall under it. But if there is no common measure among these concepts, it is impossible to interpret the word as covering all of them, because a homonymous word may not be used to convey both of its meanings at once. In that case we do not say: "This is the meaning intended by God, exalted is He." Rather we say: "It is possible that this is what is intended." As for certainty, there is no way to it here.

The second possibility: these five words are not attributes of one single thing, but of different things. In this case too there are aspects:

(First) "Those who pull out forcefully" are the bows; "those who move swiftly" are the nooses; "those who swim" are the ships; "those who race" are the horses; and "those who arrange" are the angels. This was narrated by Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib from ʿAṭāʾ.

(Second) It is reported from Mujahid that "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" are death, and that "those who race" and "those who arrange" are the angels. Ascribing the pulling, the moving, and the swimming to death is metaphorical, in the sense that they occur at its occurrence.

* * *

(Third) Qatada said: all of them are the stars, except "those who arrange," which are the angels.

The second issue: He mentioned "fa-al-sābiqāt" with the fā' (then), while the one before it has the wāw (and). There are two explanations for this:

(First) The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: this clause is a consequence of the one before it, as if it were said: "and those that swam and then raced." The fā' makes swimming the cause of racing, just as you say: "He stood up, then he left," where the fā' establishes that standing was the cause of leaving. If you said "He stood and left," you would not be making standing a cause of leaving. Al-Wahidi said: the view of the author of al-Nazm is not consistent regarding His words "fa-al-mudabbirāt amran," because it is unlikely that racing should be the cause of arranging. I say: the objection of al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, can be answered in two ways:

(First) It is not unlikely to say: when they were commanded, they swam, then raced, then arranged what they were commanded to arrange and set right. These are actions connected one to another, like your saying: "Zayd stood up, then left, then struck ʿAmr."

(Second) It is not unlikely to say: when they were foremost in performing acts of obedience and hastened to them, their trustworthiness became evident. For this reason God entrusted to them the management of part of the world.

(Second explanation) The angels are of two kinds: the chiefs and the disciples. The evidence for this is that God, glorified and exalted, said: "Say: The angel of death will take you back" (﴿قُلْ يَتَوَفّاكم مَلَكُ المَوْتِ﴾, Q. 32:11), and then said: "Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him" (﴿حَتّى إذا جاءَ أحَدَكُمُ المَوْتُ تَوَفَّتْهُ رُسُلُنا﴾, Q. 6:61). We said, in reconciling the two verses, that the angel of death is the head, and the chief and the rest of the angels are his disciples. Having understood this, we say: "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" refer to the disciples who themselves carry out the work. Then His words, exalted is He, "fa-al-sābiqāt... fa-al-mudabbirāt" are an indication of the chiefs, who are foremost in rank and nobility, and who are the arrangers of those states and works.

The first issue: Know that these five words may be attributes of one thing, and may not be so. As for the first possibility, they have mentioned several opinions regarding the verse:

(The first) that they are all attributes of the angels. So His saying ﴿By those who drag forth violently﴾ refers to the angels who pull out the souls of the children of Adam. When they pull out the soul of an unbeliever, they pull it with severity. This is derived from their saying: "nazaʿa fi al-qaws fa-aghraqa" (he drew the bowstring and over-drew it). It is said: "aghraqa al-nazii' fi al-qaws" when the archer reaches the utmost limit of the draw, until it reaches the arrow-head. So the sense of the verse is: "by those who draw with over-drawing (ighraq)." Al-gharq and al-ighraq are, in the language, of one meaning. His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾: al-nashṭ is pulling. It is said: "nashaṭtu al-dalw, unshiṭuhā, wa-anshaṭtuhā nashṭan" — I drew the bucket out gently. The meaning is the angels who draw out the soul of the believer and take it gently. We have specified this for the believer and the first for the unbeliever because of the difference between drawing violently and drawing gently: al-nazʿ is pulling with severity, and al-nashṭ is pulling with gentleness and softness. So the angels draw out the souls of the believers just as the bucket is drawn out of the well. The conclusion is that His saying ﴿By those who drag forth violently, by those who draw out gently﴾ is an oath by the Angel of Death and his assistants, except that the first indicates the manner of taking the souls of the unbelievers, and the second indicates the manner of taking the souls of the believers.

As for His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾, some have restricted it also to the angels who take souls, and some have taken it to refer to the rest of the categories of angels.

As for the first opinion, it is transmitted from ʿAlī (peace be upon him), Ibn ʿAbbās, and Masrūq that the angels draw out the souls of the believers with gentle drawing. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾. Then they leave it to rest for a while, then they extract it afterward with gentleness and delicacy, like one who swims in water, who moves gently and delicately so as not to sink. Likewise here, they are gentle in this extraction

so that pain and severity do not reach it. That is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾. As for those who took it to refer to the rest of the categories of angels, they said: the angels descend from the heaven swiftly, so their descent from the sky is made like swimming, and the Arabs say of a noble horse that it is "al-sābiḥ" (the swimmer).

As for His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾, some have explained it as the angels who take souls, who race forward with the souls of the unbelievers to the Fire, and with the souls of the believers to Paradise. Others have explained it as the rest of the categories of angels. Then they mentioned several opinions regarding this racing:

(The first) Mujahid and Abu Rawq said: the angels precede the son of Adam in faith and obedience, and there is no doubt that racing in good deeds is a great rank. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost, ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 10–11].

(The second) al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: the angels outpace the devils with revelation to the prophets, because the devils used to steal hearing.

(The third) and it is possible that the meaning is that He the Exalted described them, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 27], meaning before permission they do not move or speak, out of glorification of the majesty of Allah the Exalted and fear of His awe. Here He described them with racing, meaning when the command comes to them, they hasten to carry it out and rush to show their obedience. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾.

As for His saying ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, they agreed that they are the angels. Muqatil said: meaning Jibril, Mikail, Israfil and ʿAzrāʾīl, peace be upon them, who arrange the command of Allah the Exalted concerning the people of the earth, and they are "the distributors of affairs." As for Jibril, he is entrusted with the winds and the hosts; as for Mikail, he is entrusted with rain and plants; as for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with taking souls; as for Israfil, he descends with the command to them. Among them are a group entrusted with guarding the children of Adam, another group with recording their deeds, and another group with sinking, transformation, winds, clouds and rains.

Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: Why did He say ﴿those who arrange affairs (amran)﴾ and not "affairs (umūran)," since they arrange many affairs and not one single affair? (The answer): the intended meaning is the genus, and when it is so, it stands in place of the plural.

The second question: He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the command is all for Allah﴾, so how does He here establish for them the arranging of the affair? (The answer): since that bringing [of it] is what they do, the command is as if it were His. This is a summary of what the exegetes have said on this topic. But I have here another opinion, which is that the angels have negative attributes and relational attributes. As for the negative attributes, they are free from desire, anger, blameworthy traits, death, old age, sickness, composition of organs, humors and elements. Rather, they are spiritual substances free from these states. So His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates that they are wholly stripped of these states in every respect. On this interpretation, "al-nāziʿāt" are the ones possessing extraction, like "al-Labin" and "al-Tamir." As for His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾, it indicates that their departure from these states is not by way of obligation and hardship as with humans, but rather by the requirement of their quiddities they have departed from these states and are exalted above these attributes. These two words are thus indications describing their negative states. As for their relational attributes, they are of two kinds: (one of them) is an explanation of their intellectual faculty, that is, how their state is in knowing the kingdom and dominion of Allah and in being informed of the light of His majesty. So He described them in this station with two descriptions: (one of them) is His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾, for they glide from the beginning of their nature in the seas of Allah's majesty, and then there is no end to their gliding, because there is no end to Allah's greatness, the loftiness of His self-sufficiency, the light of His majesty and His magnificence. So they are forever in that gliding. (The second) is His saying

﴿then those who race forward﴾, which is an indication of the ranks of the angels in that gliding. For just as the ranks of the knowledge of animals compared to the ranks of the knowledge of humans are deficient, and the ranks of the knowledge of humans compared to the ranks of the knowledge of angels are deficient, so too the knowledge of some of those angels compared to the ranks of knowledge of the others varies. And just as the difference between the species of the horse and the species of the human is in quiddity and not in accidents, so too the difference between the individual of each angel and the individual of another is in quiddity. So when their individuals vary in quiddity and not in accidents, they will necessarily vary in degrees of knowledge and in levels of manifestation. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾. These two words are intended to explain the state of their intellectual faculty.

As for His saying ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, it is an indication of explaining the state of their active faculty, because every state of the lower world is entrusted to the management of one of the angels who are the inhabitants of the upper world and the dwellers of the regions of the heavens. This which I have mentioned is an apparent possibility, and Allah knows best His intended meaning in His words.

Know that Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani objected to interpreting these words as referring to the angels, and said: the singular of "al-nāziʿāt" is "nāziʿa," which is of feminine form, and Allah the Exalted has declared the angels free from femininity, and He censured the saying of the unbelievers when He said: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Gracious, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19].

We say instead that God, glorified and exalted, has made His custom to be that each of their particular states becomes a cause for a particular event in this world, just as He made eating a cause of satiety, drinking a cause of quenching thirst, and contact with fire a cause of burning. Holding this view does not harm Islam in any way whatsoever. God knows best the reality of the matter.

The third aspect in interpreting these five words is that they refer to souls (arwāḥ). This is because the soul of the dead person is pulled out (tanzi'u). One says: "So-and-so is in the throes of death (al-nazʿ)," and "So-and-so is being pulled out (yanzi'u)" when he is in the death agony (siyāq al-mawt). "The souls are pulling out (nāzi'āt) at the time of the death agony." The meaning of "gharqan" is a forceful pulling, the most intense and extreme, like the archer's drawing of the bow to its full extent (ighrāq al-nāzi' fī al-qaws). Likewise "tanshiṭu," because nashṭ means departure (al-khurūj). Then, the human souls, free of bodily attachments and longing for union with the higher realm, once they have departed from the darkness of bodies, go to the world of the angels and the abodes of holiness (qudus) in the swiftest manner, in repose and fragrance. So their departure in this state is expressed by the word "swimming" (sibāḥa). Moreover, there is no doubt that the ranks of souls differ in their aversion to this world and their love of union with the higher world. The more perfect they are in these states, the earlier their journey there; the weaker they are, the heavier their journey there. There is no doubt that the souls that are first to attain these states are the most noble. Therefore, the oath is sworn by them. Furthermore, it is not unlikely that among these noble, exalted souls there are some which, because of their strength and nobility, leave visible effects on the conditions of this world. Thus they are "those who arrange affairs" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾, "those who arrange the matter"). Does not a person see his teacher in a dream, ask him about a problem, and be guided to its solution? Does not a son see his father in a dream, and be guided to a buried treasure? Did not Galen (Jālīnūs) say: "I was sick and could not treat myself, so I saw someone in a dream who guided me to the method of treatment"? Did not al-Ghazali say: "When noble souls separate from their bodies, and then a person who resembles the first person in soul and body appears, it is not unlikely that the separated soul acquires an attachment to this body, until it becomes like a helper to the soul attached to that body in acts of goodness; and that assistance is called inspiration (ilhām)." The counterpart of this among wicked souls is whispering (waswasa). Although these meanings are not transmitted from the exegetes, the word is highly capable of bearing them.

The fourth aspect in interpreting these five words: they are attributes of the horses of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) refers to them because they pull at their reins with such force that the reins are drawn out, owing to the length of their necks, because they are purebred (ʿirāb). "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) refers to them because they leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war. It is from the expression "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) refers to them because they swim (sabaḥa) in their running. "Those who race" (sābiqāt) refers to them because they outrun to the finish. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) refers to them as arranging the matter of victory and triumph. Ascribing the arranging to them is metaphorical, because they are among its causes.

* * *

The fifth aspect, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, may God have mercy on him: these are attributes of the raiders. So "those who pull out" (nāzi'āt) are the hands of the raiders. One says of the archer "nazaʿa fī qawsihi" (he drew his bow). One says "aghraqa fi al-nazʿ" when he draws the bowstring to its full extent. "Those who move swiftly" (nāshiṭāt) are the arrows, and their movement is their leaving the hands of the archers and their penetrating. Everything you loosen (ḥalaltahu) you have made active (naššaṭtahu). From this comes nashāṭ al-rajul, which is his expansion and lightness. "Those who swim" (sābiḥāt) in this context are the horses, and their swimming is their running. It is also permissible to mean camels by it. "Those who arrange" (mudabbirāt) are like "those who follow" (muʿaqqibāt). The meaning is that, after this action, which is the pulling of arrows and the swimming and racing of horses, comes the matter which is victory. The feminine form of the word is because these are groups, as it is said "al-mudabbirāt." It is possible that what is meant is the instrument, namely the bow and the nooses, in the sense of that from which the arrow is drawn and by which the rope is loosed.

The sixth aspect: it is possible to interpret these words by the stations involved in the heart's return from other than God, exalted is He, to God. "By those who pull out forcefully" (﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾) refers to the souls that strive to grasp the firmest handhold (al-ʿurwa al-wuthqā), or those that are drawn away from love of other than God, exalted is He. "And those who move swiftly, with swiftness" (﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾) refers to the fact that, after their return from corporeal things, they begin striving and adorning themselves with the character of God, glorified and exalted, with complete energy and strong power. "And those who swim, with swimming" (﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾): then, after striving, they roam in the matter of the dominion (malakūt), and they traverse those seas and swim in them. "Then those who race, racing" (﴿فالسّابِقاتِ سَبْقًا﴾) is an indication of the differences among souls in their degrees of journeying to God, exalted is He. "Then those who arrange the matter" (﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾) is an indication that the last stage of humanity is connected to the first degree of angelhood. When human souls reach the furthest of their goals, which is the rank of racing, they are joined to the world of the angels. This is what is meant by His words: "then those who arrange the matter." So the first four are what is meant by His words: "its oil would almost give light" (﴿يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ﴾, Q. 24:35). The fifth is the fire in His words: "even if no fire had touched it" (﴿ولَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ﴾, Q. 24:35).

Know that the aspects transmitted from the exegetes are not transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explicitly, such that no addition to them is possible. Rather, they mentioned them only because the word is capable of bearing them. If the word's capacity for what we have mentioned is not less than its capacity for the aspects they mentioned, then what they mentioned is not preferable to what we mentioned. However, there is a subtle point here: the word is capable of all of them. If we find among these meanings one common concept, we interpret the word according to that common concept, and then all these aspects fall under it. But if there is no common measure among these concepts, it is impossible to interpret the word as covering all of them, because a homonymous word may not be used to convey both of its meanings at once. In that case we do not say: "This is the meaning intended by God, exalted is He." Rather we say: "It is possible that this is what is intended." As for certainty, there is no way to it here.

The second possibility: these five words are not attributes of one single thing, but of different things. In this case too there are aspects:

(First) "Those who pull out forcefully" are the bows; "those who move swiftly" are the nooses; "those who swim" are the ships; "those who race" are the horses; and "those who arrange" are the angels. This was narrated by Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib from ʿAṭāʾ.

(Second) It is reported from Mujahid that "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" are death, and that "those who race" and "those who arrange" are the angels. Ascribing the pulling, the moving, and the swimming to death is metaphorical, in the sense that they occur at its occurrence.

* * *

(Third) Qatada said: all of them are the stars, except "those who arrange," which are the angels.

The second issue: He mentioned "fa-al-sābiqāt" with the fā' (then), while the one before it has the wāw (and). There are two explanations for this:

(First) The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: this clause is a consequence of the one before it, as if it were said: "and those that swam and then raced." The fā' makes swimming the cause of racing, just as you say: "He stood up, then he left," where the fā' establishes that standing was the cause of leaving. If you said "He stood and left," you would not be making standing a cause of leaving. Al-Wahidi said: the view of the author of al-Nazm is not consistent regarding His words "fa-al-mudabbirāt amran," because it is unlikely that racing should be the cause of arranging. I say: the objection of al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, can be answered in two ways:

(First) It is not unlikely to say: when they were commanded, they swam, then raced, then arranged what they were commanded to arrange and set right. These are actions connected one to another, like your saying: "Zayd stood up, then left, then struck ʿAmr."

(Second) It is not unlikely to say: when they were foremost in performing acts of obedience and hastened to them, their trustworthiness became evident. For this reason God entrusted to them the management of part of the world.

(Second explanation) The angels are of two kinds: the chiefs and the disciples. The evidence for this is that God, glorified and exalted, said: "Say: The angel of death will take you back" (﴿قُلْ يَتَوَفّاكم مَلَكُ المَوْتِ﴾, Q. 32:11), and then said: "Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him" (﴿حَتّى إذا جاءَ أحَدَكُمُ المَوْتُ تَوَفَّتْهُ رُسُلُنا﴾, Q. 6:61). We said, in reconciling the two verses, that the angel of death is the head, and the chief and the rest of the angels are his disciples. Having understood this, we say: "those who pull out," "those who move swiftly," and "those who swim" refer to the disciples who themselves carry out the work. Then His words, exalted is He, "fa-al-sābiqāt... fa-al-mudabbirāt" are an indication of the chiefs, who are foremost in rank and nobility, and who are the arrangers of those states and works.

We have specified this for the believer and the first for the unbeliever because of the difference between drawing violently and drawing gently: al-nazʿ is pulling with severity, and al-nashṭ is pulling with gentleness and softness. The conclusion is that His saying ﴿By those who drag forth violently, by those who draw out gently﴾ is an oath by the Angel of Death and his assistants, except that the first indicates the manner of taking the souls of the unbelievers, and the second indicates the manner of taking the souls of the believers.

This is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾. Then they leave it to rest for a while, then they extract it afterward with gentleness and delicacy, like one who swims in water, who moves gently and delicately so as not to sink.
