(The second) al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: the angels outpace the devils with revelation to the prophets, because the devils used to steal hearing.

(The third) and it is possible that the meaning is that He the Exalted described them, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 27], meaning before permission they do not move or speak, out of glorification of the majesty of Allah the Exalted and fear of His awe. Here He described them with racing, meaning when the command comes to them, they hasten to carry it out and rush to show their obedience. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾.

As for His saying ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, they agreed that they are the angels. Muqatil said: meaning Jibril, Mikail, Israfil and ʿAzrāʾīl, peace be upon them, who arrange the command of Allah the Exalted concerning the people of the earth, and they are "the distributors of affairs." As for Jibril, he is entrusted with the winds and the hosts; as for Mikail, he is entrusted with rain and plants; as for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with taking souls; as for Israfil, he descends with the command to them. Among them are a group entrusted with guarding the children of Adam, another group with recording their deeds, and another group with sinking, transformation, winds, clouds and rains.

Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: Why did He say ﴿those who arrange affairs (amran)﴾ and not "affairs (umūran)," since they arrange many affairs and not one single affair? (The answer): the intended meaning is the genus, and when it is so, it stands in place of the plural.

The second question: He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the command is all for Allah﴾, so how does He here establish for them the arranging of the affair? (The answer): since that bringing [of it] is what they do, the command is as if it were His. This is a summary of what the exegetes have said on this topic. But I have here another opinion, which is that the angels have negative attributes and relational attributes. As for the negative attributes, they are free from desire, anger, blameworthy traits, death, old age, sickness, composition of organs, humors and elements. Rather, they are spiritual substances free from these states. So His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates that they are wholly stripped of these states in every respect. On this interpretation, "al-nāziʿāt" are the ones possessing extraction, like "al-Labin" and "al-Tamir." As for His saying ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾, it indicates that their departure from these states is not by way of obligation and hardship as with humans, but rather by the requirement of their quiddities they have departed from these states and are exalted above these attributes. These two words are thus indications describing their negative states. As for their relational attributes, they are of two kinds: (one of them) is an explanation of their intellectual faculty, that is, how their state is in knowing the kingdom and dominion of Allah and in being informed of the light of His majesty. So He described them in this station with two descriptions: (one of them) is His saying ﴿by those who glide swiftly﴾, for they glide from the beginning of their nature in the seas of Allah's majesty, and then there is no end to their gliding, because there is no end to Allah's greatness, the loftiness of His self-sufficiency, the light of His majesty and His magnificence. So they are forever in that gliding. (The second) is His saying

﴿then those who race forward﴾, which is an indication of the ranks of the angels in that gliding. For just as the ranks of the knowledge of animals compared to the ranks of the knowledge of humans are deficient, and the ranks of the knowledge of humans compared to the ranks of the knowledge of angels are deficient, so too the knowledge of some of those angels compared to the ranks of knowledge of the others varies. And just as the difference between the species of the horse and the species of the human is in quiddity and not in accidents, so too the difference between the individual of each angel and the individual of another is in quiddity. So when their individuals vary in quiddity and not in accidents, they will necessarily vary in degrees of knowledge and in levels of manifestation. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿then those who race forward﴾. These two words are intended to explain the state of their intellectual faculty.

As for His saying ﴿then those who arrange affairs﴾, it is an indication of explaining the state of their active faculty, because every state of the lower world is entrusted to the management of one of the angels who are the inhabitants of the upper world and the dwellers of the regions of the heavens. And since management is not completed except after knowledge, they necessarily put the explanation of the intellectual faculty they have before the explanation of the active faculty they have. This which I have mentioned is an apparent possibility, and Allah knows best His intended meaning in His words.

Know that Abu Muslim ibn Bahr al-Isfahani objected to interpreting these words as referring to the angels, and said: the singular of "al-nāziʿāt" is "nāziʿa," which is of feminine form, and Allah the Exalted has declared the angels free from femininity, and He censured the saying of the unbelievers when He said: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Gracious, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19].

(The second) that "al-nāziʿāt" derives from their saying "nazaʿa ilayhi," meaning he went with a going-out. Thus al-Wahidi said. So it is as if they rise and set by drawing and driving.

(One of them) that it be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of "al-nāziʿāt," meaning these stars are like those drowned in that drawing and intent. This is an indication of the perfection of their state in that intent. If it is said: if the spheres and stars are not living rational beings, what is the meaning of describing them thus? We say: this is by way of comparison, like His saying: ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Yasin: 40], for the plural with waw and nun is for rational beings, and then it was mentioned of the stars by way of comparison.

(The second) that the meaning of their "drowning" is their disappearance in the horizon of the west. So "al-nāziʿāt" is an indication of their rising, and "gharqan" is an indication of their setting, that is, they draw and then are drowned with drowning. This aspect has been mentioned by a group of exegetes.

As for His saying ﴿and those who glide swiftly, gliding (nashṭan)﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: its meaning is that they go out from one mansion to another, from your saying: "a bull that is nāshiṭ" when it leaves one land for another. I say: the upshot of this statement returns to: His saying ﴿by those who drag forth violently﴾ indicates their daily motion, and ﴿by those who draw out gently﴾ indicates their movement from one mansion to another, which is their particular motion in their own spheres. And it is remarkable that their daily motions are compulsory, while their motion from mansion to mansion is not compulsory, but

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 79, verses 6–9:

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿On the day the quaker quakes﴾ ﴿Followed by the follower﴾ ﴿Hearts that day will be trembling﴾ ﴿Their eyes humbled.﴾ On this there are several questions.

**Question 1:** Is the answer to the preceding oath omitted, or is it stated? On this there are two views.

**(The first view)** It is omitted. On this view there are several possibilities for the verse.

**The first:** al-Farra' said the implied answer is "You will surely be resurrected" (la-tub'athunna). The evidence for this is what God relates of them, that they said: ﴿When we have become decayed bones, shall we really be raised?﴾ That is, "Shall we be raised when we have become decayed bones?"

**The second:** al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said the implied answer is "We will surely blow into the Trumpet twice" (la-nanfakhanna fi al-sur nafkhatayn). The omitted part is indicated by the mention of the quaker (al-raajifa) and the follower (al-raadifa), which are the two blasts.

**The third:** al-Kisa'i said the implied answer is that the Resurrection is certainly coming. This is because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿By the winnowing winds﴾ and then said: ﴿What you are promised is surely true﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 5]. He also said: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ ... ﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1, 7]. So it is the same here, since the Qur'an is like a single surah.

**(The second view)** The answer is stated. On this view there are several possibilities:

**The first:** The thing sworn to is His saying: ﴿Hearts that day will be trembling, their eyes humbled.﴾ The meaning is: "By those who pull out violently, on the day the quaker quakes, hearts will be trembling and their eyes humbled."

**The second:** The answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 15]. Here "hal" carries the meaning of "qad" (indeed), as in His saying: ﴿Has the news of the Overwhelming reached you?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 1], meaning "Indeed the news of the Overwhelming has reached you."

**The third:** The answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26]

**Question 2:** Regarding the governing element of (yawma, "on the day"), there are two views:

**(One of them)** It is governed by the implied answer. The meaning is: "You will surely be raised on the day the quaker quakes." If it is asked: "How is this valid, since they will not be raised at the first blast, and the quaker is the first blast?" We answer: The meaning is that they will be raised within the extended period during which the two blasts occur. There is no doubt that they will be raised in part of that extended period, namely the time of the second blast. The evidence for what we have said is that His saying ﴿followed by the follower﴾ is made a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the quaker.

**(The other)** (yawma tarjufu) is governed by what is indicated by ﴿Hearts that day will be trembling﴾, meaning: "On the day the quaker quakes, hearts will have trembled."

**Question 3:** The word (al-rajfah) in the language may bear two meanings:

**(One of them)** Movement, as in His saying: ﴿On the day the earth and mountains quake﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14].

**(The other)** A terrifying crash and a fearsome sound, from the expression "rajafa al-ra'd yarjufu rajfan wa rajifan" (the thunder rumbled), which refers to the repeated reverberation of its dreadful sounds and its echoing in the clouds. From the same root is His saying: ﴿the earthquake seized them﴾ [al-A'raf: 78]. On this meaning, the quaker is a great cry containing terror and severity, like thunder. As for the follower, it is anything that comes after something else; one says "radifahu," meaning "he came after him." As for the trembling hearts (al-qulub al-wajifah), they are those that are agitated and fearful. One says "wajafa qalbuhu yajifu wijafan" when it is agitated, and from it comes "ijaf al-dabbah," which means urging the animal to move at a fast pace. The exegetes have given many expressions for the meaning of "wajifah," and all of them amount to the same thing. They said: fearful and anxious, leaping out of their places, restless, agitated, violently disturbed, not still. Their owners' eyes are humbled. This is like His saying: ﴿humbled by disgrace, they look with furtive glances﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

Having established this, we say: The majority of exegetes agree that these matters are the conditions of the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani claimed that this is not so. We will mention the exegetes' interpretations and then explain Abu Muslim's view.

As for the first view, which is the well-known view among the majority, that these conditions are those of the Day of Resurrection, they gave several interpretations:

**(The first)** The quaker is the first blast. It was so named either because the world is shaken and agitated at it, or because the sound of that blast is the quaker, as we explained. The follower is another quake that follows the first, when the earth trembles to bring the dead back to life, just as it trembled in the first for the death of the living, as God mentions in Surah al-Zumar. It is also related from the Messenger (ﷺ) that between the two blasts there will be forty years. It is related that during these forty years God will send rain upon the earth, and that water will come upon it like seeds, and that this is like the means for bringing the living back. This is something not needed for the Return, but God may do what He wills and decree what He desires.

**(The second)** The quaker is the first blast, and the follower is the arrival of the Hour, from His saying: ﴿It may be that some of what you seek to hasten has drawn close to you﴾ [al-Naml: 72]. That is, the Resurrection which the disbelievers seek to hasten in disbelief of it. It "follows" them because it is near.

**(The third)** The quaker is the earth and the mountains, from His saying: ﴿the day the earth and mountains quake﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14]. The follower is the sky and the stars, because they split and their stars scatter in its wake.

**(The fourth)** The quaker is the earth, which moves and is shaken, and the follower is a second earthquake that follows the first, until the earth is torn apart and destroyed.

**(The second view)** This is the view of Abu Muslim: that these conditions are not those of the Day of Resurrection. This is because it has been reported from him that he interpreted "al-nazi'at" as "pulling the bowstring," "al-nashitat" as "the release of the arrow," "al-sabihat" as "the running of the horse," "al-sabiqat" as "its outstripping," and "al-mudabbirat" as "the affairs that occur after that shooting and running." He then built upon this and said: The quaker is the horses of the polytheists, and likewise the follower. By this is meant two groups of polytheists who raided the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and one of them outran the other. The trembling hearts are those that are anxious, and the humbled eyes are the eyes of the hypocrites, like His saying: ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease look at you with the gaze of one fainting from death﴾ [Muhammad: 20]. It is as if it were said: When the enemy's horses came, quaking, and their sister followed them, the hearts of the hypocrites trembled with fear, and their eyes were humbled through cowardice and weakness. Then they said: ﴿Shall we really be returned to the former state?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10], meaning: "Shall we return to the world so that we may bear this fear for its sake?" They also said: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 12]. So the beginning of this speech relates the condition of the polytheists who raided the Messenger of God (ﷺ), its middle relates the condition of the hypocrites, and its end relates the words of the hypocrites denying the Gathering. Then He, glorified and exalted, answered their words by saying: ﴿It will be but a single cry﴾ ﴿and at once they will be on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13–14]. This is Abu Muslim's view. The wording can bear it, although it runs contrary to the view of the majority.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Hearts that day will be trembling, their eyes humbled.﴾ Know that He did not say "the hearts that day are trembling," because it has been established by evidence that the people of faith do not fear. Rather, what is meant is the hearts of the disbelievers. What confirms this is that He related of them that they say: ﴿Shall we really be returned to the former state?﴾, and this is the speech of disbelievers, not believers. And His saying ﴿their eyes humbled﴾ is because what is known of the condition of one who is agitated and fearful is that his gaze is that of one who is humbled, abject, submissive, awaiting the great matter that is about to befall him. In the verse there are two questions:

**First question:** How is it permissible to begin with an indefinite noun? **(Answer)** (qulubun, "hearts") is in the nominative as the subject of the sentence, (wajifatun) is its adjective, and (absaruha khashi'ah) is its predicate. It is like His saying: ﴿A believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221].

**Second question:** How is it valid to attribute (absar, "eyes") to (qulub, "hearts")? **(Answer)** Its meaning is "the eyes of their owners," as is shown by His saying (yaqulun, "they say"). Next, know that here God, exalted is He, relates three statements made by those who deny the Resurrection.

The third issue: Know that the gist of this objection is that the thing each person refers to with his saying "I" is this body constructed with this particular structure. So when a person dies, his temperament (*mizaj*) is destroyed and his composition corrupted, and so his restoration is impossible, for several reasons:

(One) The returned person is not the first person unless the first composition enters existence again. That is an affirmation of the return of the very same thing that was annihilated at first, and this is impossible, because what was annihilated retains no essence, no self, and no particularity. So if something else enters existence, it is impossible to say that the returned thing is the very same as what perished at first.

(Two) Those parts become dust, scatter, and mix with the parts of all the earth, all the water, and all the air. So distinguishing those parts by their very identities from all these things is impossible.

(Three) Dust-parts are cold, dry, and harsh (*qashifa*). So the generation of a human being, who must be warm and moist in his temperament, from them is impossible. This is the full statement of the argument of those who argued for the denial of resurrection with their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed, when we are bones, decayed?﴾

The answer to this objection has several aspects. The first, and the strongest, is: We do not grant that what is pointed to by each person with his saying "I am this structure" is what he means. Then, what shows its corruption are two aspects:

The first: The parts of this structure are in melting and change, while what each person refers to with his saying "I" is not in change, and what changes is different from what does not change.

The second: A person may know that he is himself while being unaware of his outer and inner limbs, and what is perceived is different from what is not perceived. Otherwise, negation and affirmation would coincide on one thing, which is impossible. Thus it is established that what is pointed to by each person with his saying "I" is not this structure.

Then here there are three possibilities:

One: That thing is an existent that subsists by itself, neither a body nor bodily, according to the view of a great group of philosophers and Muslims.

Two: That it is a body differing in quiddity from these bodies, which are subject to dissolution and corruption, pervading them as fire pervades charcoal, oil pervades sesame, and rosewater pervades the rose. So when this structure corrupts, those parts contract and remain alive, perceiving and rational, either in wretchedness or in happiness.

Three: It is said that it is a body equal to these bodies in quiddity, except that God, exalted is He, has specified it for permanence and continuance from the first state of a person's coming into existence until the end of his life. As for the other changing parts, which sometimes increase and sometimes decrease, they are not included in what is pointed to by his saying "I." So at death those parts separate, and that thing remains alive, either in happiness or in wretchedness.

When these possibilities have appeared, it is established that the corruption of the body and the scattering of its parts does not necessitate the corruption of what the human being truly is. This is a fine and firm position, by which all the doubts of the deniers of resurrection are cut off. On this supposition, the becoming of the bones decayed, rotten, and scattered has absolutely no effect in refuting gathering and raising.

Suppose, for the sake of argument, that we grant that the human being is the totality of this structure. Then why do you say that restoration is impossible? Your saying: "What is annihilated is not restored." We say: Is it not the case that, in its state of non-existence, according to you, it was not impossible to make a judgment about it that its return is impossible? So why should it not be that, according to our view too, it is not impossible to make a judgment about it that its return is possible?

Your saying, secondly: "The few parts are mixed with the parts of the four elements." We say: But it is established that the Creator of the world knows all particulars and is capable of all possibilities, so it is valid for Him to gather them in their very identities and restore life to them.

Your saying, thirdly: "Dry, harsh bodies do not accept life." We say: We see the salamander living in fire, the ostrich swallowing a heated iron piece, and great large snakes generated in snow. So reliance on induction is refuted. And God is the guide to truth and right.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 79, verses 15–17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa﴾ ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ In this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the connection between this story and what precedes it is in two respects. The first: He, exalted is He, related the persistence of the disbelievers in denying the Resurrection, to the point that they reached the degree of mockery in their saying: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return.﴾ This grieved Muhammad (ﷺ), so He mentioned the story of Moses, peace be upon him, and showed that he bore great hardship in calling Pharaoh, so that this would serve as consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ). The second: Pharaoh was stronger than the disbelievers of Quraysh, more numerous in company, and more formidable in might. When he rebelled against Moses, God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the present life. Likewise, these polytheists, in their rebellion against you, if they persist, God will seize them and make them an example.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿Has it reached you?﴾ may mean: Has it not indeed reached you, ﴿the story of Moses?﴾ This is if it had reached him before this statement. But if it had not reached him, it may be said: ﴿Has it reached you?﴾ such-and-such, or shall I inform you of it? For in it is a lesson for whoever fears.

The third issue: The sacred valley is the blessed, purified valley. Concerning His saying (Tuwa) there are several views:

One: It is the name of a valley in Syria, near the Mount (al-Tur) by which God swore in His saying: (By the Mount) ﴿and a written Book﴾ [al-Tur: 1–2], and His saying: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the Mount﴾ [Maryam: 52].

Second: It means, in Hebrew, "O man," so it is as if He said: O man, ﴿go to Pharaoh﴾. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Third: His saying (Tuwa) means: He called him at Tuwa of the night, ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾, because you say: I came to you after Tuwa, meaning after an hour of the night.

Fourth: The meaning is: the sacred valley that was folded (tuwiya), i.e., blessed twice.

The fourth issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "Tuwa" with a dammah on the ta', without tanwin. The rest read it with a dammah on the ta' with tanwin. It is also narrated from Abu 'Amr: Tiwa with a kasrah on the ta', and Tuwa like Thana. Both are names for the folded thing, and at-tayy means folding (ath-thany), i.e., I folded it in blessing and sanctification. Al-Farra' said: "Tuwa" is a valley between Medina and Egypt. Whoever gives it tanwin says it is masculine, and we named it as a masculine name. Whoever does not give it tanwin treats it as diptote, deviating from its original form, like 'Umar and Zufar. Then he said: Tanwin is more beloved to me, since I did not find in the deviated forms a parallel, meaning I did not find a noun from waw and ya' that was shifted from its active form to a verb other than (Tuwa).

The fifth issue: The estimated sense of the verse: ﴿when his Lord called to him and said: Go to Pharaoh.﴾ In the reading of Abdullah: ﴿that go﴾, because in calling there is the meaning of saying. As for whether that calling was by making the eternal speech heard, or by making a letter and sound heard, and if it was in this way, how did Moses know that it was the speech of God? All of that has already been discussed in Surah Ta-Ha.

The sixth issue: The other verses indicate that when God first called Moses, peace be upon him, He mentioned to him many things, as in His saying in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿O Moses, I am your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 11–12], up to His saying: ﴿that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ This shows that His saying here: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾ is among what his Lord called him with, not that it is all that He called him with. Also, the purpose is not that he, peace be upon him, was sent only to Pharaoh, but to everyone in that region; he specified him by mention because his call was like the call of all that people.

The seventh issue: Transgression (at-tughyan) is exceeding the limit. Then, He, exalted is He, did not state in what he exceeded, so some exegetes said: its meaning is that he was arrogant toward God and disbelieved in Him, and others said: he transgressed against the Children of Israel. My view is that the better course is to combine both matters: the meaning is that he transgressed against the Creator by disbelieving in Him, and transgressed against the creation by being arrogant toward them and enslaving them. Just as the perfection of servitude is nothing but sincerity in dealing with the Creator and with creation, so too the perfection of transgression is nothing but combining bad dealing with the Creator and with creation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 79, verse 18:

The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: It is said, "Hal laka fi kadha?" and "Hal laka ila kadha?" just as you say, "Are you inclined to it?" and "Are you inclined toward it?" Al-Wahidi said: the subject is elided in wording but intended in meaning, and the estimate is: "Hal laka ila an tazakka hajatun aw irbatun?" (Is there for you a need or a purpose in purifying yourself?). The poet said:

"Fa-hal lakum fiha ilayya fa-innani / basirun bima a'ya al-nitasiyya hidhayma"
(So is there for you in it, toward me? For I am one who sees what baffled the physician Hidhyam.)

It is also possible that the estimate is: "Hal laka sabilun ila an tazakka?" (Is there for you a way to purify yourself?).

The second issue: Zakiyy means pure, free from all defects. He said: ﴿Have you killed an innocent soul?﴾ [al-Kahf: 74], and He said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. This word encompasses everything to which he is being called, because the meaning is: "Is there for you a way to do that by which you become pure from everything that is not fitting?" and that is achieved by gathering everything connected with tawhid and the sharia.

The third issue: There are two readings: the doubled (tashdid) reading, by assimilating the ta' of the tafa''ul form into the zay because of their proximity, and the light (takhfif) reading.

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazilah relied on this verse to refute the claim that God the Exalted is the creator of the servant's act. This is because it is an interrogative in the form of an affirmation, meaning: "There is a way for you to purify yourself." And if that were by God the Exalted's act, the speech would be reversed upon Moses. The answer to such objections has already been given.

The fifth issue: When He said to the two of them: ﴿Speak to him with gentle words﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], it is as if He arranged for them that soft, gentle speech. This indicates that in calling to God there must be gentleness, kindness, and the abandonment of harshness. For this reason He said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. It also indicates that those who treat people roughly and go to extremes in partisanship are, as it were, opposed to what God commanded His prophets and messengers.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

Issue One: Those who hold that the knowledge of God is only attained through a guide have relied upon this verse, and they said: It is explicit that He guides him to the knowledge of God. Then they said: Among the things that show that this is the greatest purpose of sending the messengers are two matters. The first: His saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ encompasses all the matters that the one addressed must have, and this guidance is included within it. So when He repeated it after that, it became known that it is the greatest purpose of the mission. The second: Moses concluded his speech with it, and this also draws attention to its being the most noble of the purposes of the mission. The response: We do not deny that instruction and indication may be an aid in uncovering the truth. The dispute is only that you say: its attainment is impossible except from the teacher, and we do not accept that.

Issue Two: The verse indicates that the knowledge of God precedes obedience to Him, because He mentioned the guidance and made the fear subsequent to it and dependent upon it. A parallel to this is the saying of God, exalted, at the beginning of al-Nahl: ﴿That there is no god but I, so fear Me﴾ [al-Nahl: 2], and in Ta Ha: ﴿Indeed, I am God; there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾ [Ta Ha: 14].

The Exalted said: ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾, and in this there are two issues:

One: when he saw the serpent, he turned back fearful, hastening in his walk. Al-Hasan said: he was a hasty, flighty man.

Two: he turned away from Musa, striving and working hard at plotting against him.

Three: the meaning may be: then he came forward, striving, as one says: "So-and-so came forward to do such-and-such," meaning he began to do it. So "turned back" was put in the place of "came forward" so that he would not be described as advancing.

Third: His saying: ﴿So he gathered (his people) and proclaimed, and said: "I am your lord, the most high"﴾. "So he gathered" means he assembled the magicians, like His saying: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers﴾. "And proclaimed" means he proclaimed at the gathering in which they were assembled with him, or he commanded a herald who proclaimed among the people with that. It was also said: he stood among them as an orator and said that phrase. The first issue: they mentioned two views regarding the accusative of "nakal" (punishment). The first: al-Zajjaj said it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar), because the meaning of "God seized him" is "God punished him with punishment (nakal) of the Hereafter and the first," since "seized" and "punished" are close in meaning; and it is like saying "I leave him with a severe leaving," because "leave" and "abandon" are the same. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe﴾ [Hud: 102]. The second: al-Farra' said: he means "God seized him with a seizure that is a punishment (nakal) for the Hereafter and the first," and "nakal" has the sense of "tankil" (exemplary punishment), as "salam" has the sense of "taslim."

The second issue: the exegetes mentioned several interpretations of this verse:

One: that "the Hereafter and the first" are attributes of Pharaoh's two statements: one is his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾, and the other is his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾. They said: between them were forty years. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil, and the narration of 'Ata' and al-Kalbi from Ibn 'Abbas. The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that He did not seize him immediately for his first statement, but gave him respite for forty years; then when he uttered the second, he was seized for both. This is a reminder that He, exalted is He, gives respite but does not neglect.

Two: this is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah: ﴿the punishment of the Hereafter and the first﴾, meaning He punished him in the Hereafter and drowned him in this world.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 79, verse 26–28 (part 1 of 2):

Then, Exalted is He, concluded this story with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾. The meaning is that in what We have related of the matter of Musa and Fir'awn, and what Allah brought down upon Fir'awn of disgrace, and granted Musa of elevation and victory, there is a lesson for whoever fears, namely that he should abandon rebellion against Allah, Exalted is He, and denial of His prophets, out of fear that what befell Fir'awn may befall him, and out of knowledge that Allah, Exalted is He, supports His prophets and messengers. So take heed, O assemblies of those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ), by what we have mentioned; that is, know that if you share with them in the meaning that draws punishment, you will share with them in the descent of punishment upon you.

Then know that when He, Exalted is He, concluded this story, He returned to addressing the deniers of resurrection, and said: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the sky?﴾ And in this there are two issues:

The first issue: Concerning the purpose of this argument, there are two views:

The first: It is an argument against the deniers of resurrection, when He said: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the sky?﴾, drawing their attention to a matter known by observation. This is because the creation of man, despite his smallness and weakness, when compared with the creation of the sky with its greatness and the greatness of its conditions, is slight. So He, Exalted is He, made clear that the creation of the sky is greater. And if that is so, then their creation in the manner of re-creation is more fitting to be within Allah's power, so how can they deny it? A similar verse is His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81], and His saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. The meaning is: Is your creation after death more difficult, or the creation of the sky, that is, in your estimation and reckoning? For both matters are equal in relation to the power of Allah.

The second: The purpose of this argument is to show that they are created beings. This view is weak for two reasons:

One of them: whoever denies that man is created, it is more fitting that he would deny it regarding the sky.

The second: the beginning of the surah was concerning the issue of gathering and resurrection, so it is more appropriate to interpret this statement in that light.

The second issue: Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: this speech is complete at His saying: ﴿or is the sky?﴾, and then His saying, Exalted is He: (He built it) begins another statement. But according to Abu Hatim, the pause is at His saying: (He built it). He said: because it is a relative clause of "the sky", and the sense is: "or the sky which He built", so the "which" (alladhi) was omitted, and such omission is permissible. Al-Qaffal said: It is said: "The man who came to you is intelligent", that is, "the man who came to you is intelligent". Once it is established that this is permissible in the language, we say: The evidence that His saying (He built it) is a relative clause of what precedes it is that if it were not a relative clause, it would be a qualifier, and His saying (He built it) would be a qualifier; then His saying ﴿He raised its height﴾ is a qualifier, so two qualifiers would follow one another with no connection between them, and it would have been necessary to insert a conjunction between them, as in His saying: ﴿and He made dark its night﴾. Since that is not the case, we know that His saying (He built it) is a relative clause for "the sky". Then He said: ﴿He raised its height﴾ as a new beginning, mentioning its attribute. Al-Farra' may argue for his view that if His saying (He built it) were a relative clause for "the sky", the sense would be: "or the sky [which] He built", and this would imply the existence of some sky which Allah did not build, and that is false.

The third issue: What indicates that He, Exalted is He, is the One who built the sky are several proofs:

One of them: The sky is a body, and every body is originated; for if the body were eternal, then in eternity it would be either moving or at rest, and both alternatives are false, so the claim that the body is eternal is false. As for the restriction, it is because it is either settled where it is, and then it is at rest, or it is not settled where it is, and then it is moving. We say that it is impossible for it to be moving because the quiddity of motion requires being preceded by something else, and the quiddity of eternity contradicts being preceded by something else, and combining the two is impossible. And we say that it is impossible for it to be at rest because rest is an affirmative attribute, and it is capable of ceasing, and everything capable of ceasing is in need of a free agent, and everything of that kind is originated; so every rest is originated, and it is impossible for it to be eternal. We say that rest is an affirmative attribute because the body's state changes from moving to resting while its essence remains; so one of the two must necessarily be an affirmative matter. If the affirmative matter is rest, the aim is achieved; and if the affirmative matter is motion, it is also necessary that rest be affirmative, because motion is the state of being in a place after having been in another, and rest is the state of being in a place after having been in that same place; so the difference between motion and rest is not in the quiddity but in being preceded by something else and not being preceded by something else. That is an accidental, external attribute outside the quiddity. And if that is so, then once it is established that this quiddity is an existential matter in one of the two forms, it must be so in another form. We say that the rest of the sky is capable of ceasing, because if it were necessary in its essence, its cessation would be impossible, and so the sky would not be moving; but we see it now moving, so we know that if it had been at rest in eternity, that rest would have been capable of ceasing. We say that since that rest is possible in its essence, it requires a free agent, for since it is possible in its essence, it must have an effector; and that effector cannot be a necessitating cause, for if that necessitating cause were necessary, and independent in its necessitating that effect from any condition, then its permanence would entail the permanence of that effect, and so it would have to not cease for rest; and if it were necessary but needing for its necessitating of that effect a condition that is necessary in its essence, then the permanence of the cause and the permanence of the condition would entail the permanence of the effect. As for if the necessitating cause is not necessary in its essence, or the condition of its necessitating is not necessary in its essence, then the discussion of it is like the discussion of the first, and an infinite regress follows, which is impossible, or one reaches a necessitating cause necessary in its essence and a condition necessary in its essence, and then the first objection returns. Thus it is established that that effector must necessarily be a free agent. Then every rest is an act of a free agent, and everything of that kind is originated, because the one who chooses acts only through intention, and intending the bringing into being of what already exists, and obtaining what is already obtained, is impossible. Thus it is established that every rest is originated. It is therefore established that it is impossible for the body to be in eternity neither moving nor at rest; so it is not existent in eternity, and so it is originated. And if it is originated, it requires in its essence and in the composition of its parts a originator, and that is Allah, Exalted is He. Thus it is established by reason that the builder of the sky is Allah, Exalted is He.

The second proof: Everything other than the Necessary Being is possible, every possible thing is originated, and every originated thing has a maker. We say: everything other than the Necessary Being is possible, because if we supposed two beings each necessary in its own essence, they would share in existence and be distinguished by specification, so each of them would be composed of that by which they share and that by which they are distinguished; and every composite depends on its parts, and its part is other than it; so every composite depends on something other than itself, and everything dependent on something other than itself is possible in its essence. So each of the two necessary beings in essence would be possible in essence, and this is a contradiction. Then the discussion is carried over to those two parts: if they were necessary, each of those parts would be composite, and an infinite regress follows; and if they were not necessary, then what depends on them is more deserving of non-existence. Thus it is established that what is other than the Necessary Being is possible, and every possible thing has an effector, and everything that needs an effector is originated; because the need for an effector cannot be realized in the state of subsistence, since it is impossible for the existent to bring itself into being; so it must be either in the state of coming into being or in the state of non-existence, and on either assumption, origination is necessary. Thus it is established that what is other than the Necessary Being is originated, and everything originated must have an originator; so the sky must have a builder.

The third proof: Sound reason testifies that the mass of the sky is not impossible to be larger than it is now by the size of a mustard seed, nor impossible to be smaller by the size of a mustard seed. So the specification of this particular quantity to occur, rather than a greater or lesser one, must be due to a specifier. Thus it is established that the sky must have a builder. (If it is said): Why is it not permissible to say that He created a thing and gave it a power by which that created thing can create bodies, so that the creator and builder of the sky is that thing?

The answer: Some scholars said: What is known by reason is that the sky must have an originator, and that there must ultimately be a halt at an eternal being, and the God is eternal, necessary in existence in His essence, one, and He is Allah, glorified and exalted. As for the negation of an intermediary, it is known only by revelation, and His saying in this verse: (He built it) indicates that the builder of the sky is Allah and no other. And some said: Rather, reason indicates its invalidity, because once it is established that everything other than Him is originated, it is established that He is capable, not an necessitating cause; and that which is capable of being willed by Him is possible only by virtue of being possible; for if you removed possibility, there would remain necessity or impossibility, and these two nullify being capable of being willed. And since what makes it valid for some to be willed by Allah is possibility, and possibility is general among possibilities, it must be that the validity of being willed by Allah, Exalted is He, obtains in all possibilities. And once that is established, and the relation of His power to all is equal, it must be that He is capable of all. And once it is established that Allah is capable of possibilities, if we supposed another capable being who could act upon some possibilities, it would entail one single object of power being between two capable beings from one single aspect; and that is impossible, because it either occurs by one of them rather than the other, which is impossible, since when both are independently sufficient for the effect, its occurring by this one is no more fitting than its occurring by that one or by both together; and the latter is also impossible, because then each of them would be independent of each of them, so it would be both needing and not needing both at once, which is impossible. Thus it is established by this that it is impossible for another possible thing to occur through another cause apart from the power of Allah, Exalted is He. This discourse is sound, but according to the view of those who do not affirm any effector in existence other than the One; this is the sum of what is in this chapter.

Know that when He, Exalted is He, made clear regarding the sky that He built it, He then made clear how He built it, explaining that manner from several aspects:

The first of them: what relates to place. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He raised its height﴾.

Know that when the extension of a thing is taken from its top down to its bottom, it is called depth ('umq), and when taken from its bottom up to its top, it is called height (samk). So the meaning of raising its height is the great loftiness of it, to the extent that they mentioned that between the earth and it is a journey of five hundred years. The astronomers have explained the magnitudes of the celestial bodies and the distances between each of them and the earth. Others said: rather, the meaning is: He raised its height without pillars, and that cannot be accomplished except by Allah, Exalted is He.

The second attribute: His saying, Exalted is He: (and He leveled it). Regarding this there are two views:

The first view: the meaning is the evenness of its composition. It has been said, rather, that the meaning is the negation of rifts in it, like His saying: ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Mulk: 3]. Those who hold the first view said: "fa-sawwaha" (﴿and made it even﴾) is general, so it is not permissible to restrict it to evenness in some things only. Then they said: this indicates that the heaven is a sphere (kurah), because if it were not a sphere, some of its sides would be a plane surface, some a corner, and some a line, and some of its parts would be nearer to us and some farther. Then true evenness would not be achieved. Therefore it must be a sphere, so that true evenness is achieved. Then they said: since it has been established that it is originated (muhdath), in need of a choosing agent (fa'il mukhtar), what harm to the religion arises from its being a sphere?

Know that when the Exalted, by rational proof, demonstrated the possibility of the Resurrection, then informed of its occurrence, then mentioned its general conditions, then mentioned the conditions of the wretched and the happy therein, He said, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time?﴾.

Know that the polytheists used to hear the affirmation of the Resurrection and its description with terrifying attributes, such as that it is "the Overwhelming Calamity," "the Deafening Blast," and "the Striking Calamity." So they said, by way of mockery: ﴿When is its appointed time?﴾. It is possible that this was meant to create doubt among their followers that there is no basis for it. It is also possible that they were asking the Messenger about the time of the Resurrection out of haste, as in His saying: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Shura: 18]. Then, regarding His saying "(its appointed time)" (mursaha), there are two views. The first: "When is its settling," i.e., its establishment; they meant, "When will Allah establish it, bring it into existence and bring it about?" The second: "(Ayyan)" its final end and its resting place, just as the mooring of a ship is its resting place where it comes to rest.

Then Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿In what are you concerned with mentioning it?﴾ and in this there are two views.

The first: its meaning is, "About what are you occupied with mentioning its time for them and clarifying that specific time for them?" A parallel to this is the saying of someone who, when a man asks him about something unfitting for him, says: "What is it to you and this? What business do you have with this?" And from Aisha: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, did not cease to mention the Hour and ask about it until this verse was revealed." On this view, it is an expression of wonder at how often he mentioned it, as if it were said: "In what preoccupation and concern are you with mentioning it and asking about it?" The meaning is that they ask you about it, so out of your eagerness to answer them you do not cease to mention it and ask about it.

* * *
Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿To your Lord belongs its finality﴾, i.e., the final knowledge of it; He has not given it to any of His creation. The second view: some of them said: "(In what)" is a denial of their question, i.e., "In what is this question?" Then it was said: ﴿You are of its mention﴾, i.e., He sent you, and you are the Seal of the Prophets and the last of the Messengers in mention, from among the kinds of its signs and one of the categories of its portents; so that suffices them as proof of its nearness and of the obligation to prepare for it, and there is no benefit in their asking about it.

* * *
Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾. In this there are issues:

The first issue: the meaning of the verse is that you were only sent as a warner, and this meaning does not depend on your knowledge of the time of the Hour's establishment. Rather, if we are fair, we would say that warning and frightening are only complete when knowledge of the time of the Hour's establishment is not attained.

The second issue: he, upon whom be prayer and peace, is a warner to all, but he was specified for those who fear, because they are the ones who benefit from that warning.

The third issue: it has been read as "mundhirun" with tanwin, which is the original form. Al-Zajjaj said: the forms mufʿil and fāʿil, when each of them refers to the future or the present, take tanwin, because it then stands in place of the verb, and the verb is only indefinite; the tanwin may also be dropped for lightness. Both are suitable for the present and the future. But when the past is intended, only the idafa (construction) is permitted, as in the saying "he is the warner of Zayd yesterday."
